category: Set up and configure Azure Databricks

documents.title: Choose a compute type
documents.content: Compute choices shape each workload. Azure Databricks provides job, serverless, classic, and shared compute plus SQL warehouses, letting engineers match isolation, startup time, scalability, and cost to processing requirements.

documents.title: Configure compute performance
documents.content: Performance starts with sizing. Configure CPU capacity, node type, worker count, cluster size, autoscaling ranges, automatic termination, and pools to meet processing demand without paying for unnecessary idle resources.

documents.title: Configure compute features
documents.content: Compute features tune execution. Select an Azure Databricks Runtime and Apache Spark version, enable Photon acceleration for supported SQL workloads, and choose machine learning runtimes when preinstalled ML libraries are required.

documents.title: Manage compute libraries and permissions
documents.content: Compute must be usable and controlled. Install workspace, package-repository, or custom libraries on compatible resources, then grant appropriate permissions so authorized users can attach, restart, manage, or run workloads.

documents.title: Organize catalogs with naming conventions
documents.content: Clear naming supports governance. Design catalogs around teams, domains, environments, isolation requirements, and external sharing boundaries, then create each catalog with ownership and managed storage appropriate to its purpose.

documents.title: Create schemas and volumes
documents.content: Schemas and volumes organize assets. Schemas group tables, views, functions, and models within catalogs, while Unity Catalog volumes provide governed storage for non-tabular files using the three-level namespace.

documents.title: Create tables and views
documents.content: Tables and views expose governed data. Create managed or external tables, standard views, and materialized views, and use data definition language operations to alter, replace, describe, or remove these objects.

documents.title: Connect external catalogs and configure Genie
documents.content: External discovery broadens the lakehouse. Configure connections and foreign catalogs for federated sources, then provide AI/BI Genie instructions, descriptions, and example queries that help users discover and interpret trusted data.

category: Secure and govern Unity Catalog objects

documents.title: Grant Unity Catalog privileges
documents.content: Privileges control governed assets. Grant the minimum required permissions on catalogs, schemas, tables, views, volumes, and other securable objects to users, groups, or service principals while accounting for inherited access.

documents.title: Implement fine-grained data access
documents.content: Fine-grained controls limit exposure. Combine table permissions, column-level restrictions, row-level security, and dynamic views so each principal can query only the records and attributes permitted by policy.

documents.title: Use Azure Key Vault secrets
documents.content: Secrets should remain outside code. Use Azure Key Vault-backed secret scopes to retrieve credentials from notebooks and jobs without embedding sensitive values in source files, parameters, or visible configuration.

documents.title: Authenticate automated data access
documents.content: Automation needs durable identity. Service principals authenticate unattended data operations, while managed identities access supported Azure resources without stored credentials, reducing secret rotation and accidental credential disclosure.

documents.title: Document data and apply ABAC
documents.content: Metadata makes assets understandable. Preserve table and column descriptions for discovery, apply governed tags to data objects, and use attribute-based access control policies to enforce scalable rules based on those attributes.

documents.title: Apply filters, masks, and retention policies
documents.content: Policies protect data throughout its life. Row filters tailor visible records, column masks obscure sensitive values, and retention rules determine how long regulated or operational data remains available.

documents.title: Track lineage and audit activity
documents.content: Governance requires traceability. Catalog Explorer reveals owners, history, dependencies, and lineage across assets, while audit logs record platform activity for investigation, compliance reporting, and security monitoring.

documents.title: Share data with Delta Sharing
documents.content: Delta Sharing exchanges data securely. Design shares, recipients, authentication, object selection, and revocation around business requirements so external consumers receive controlled access without copying credentials or exposing the source workspace.

documents.title: Design data ingestion logic
documents.content: Ingestion begins with source analysis. Design extraction logic around source capabilities, full or incremental loads, file types, arrival patterns, latency, volume, and the destination model required by downstream consumers.

documents.title: Choose a data ingestion tool
documents.content: The right tool reduces complexity. Choose Lakeflow Connect for managed connectors, notebooks for custom processing, or Azure Data Factory for broader integration and orchestration based on source, transformation, and operations needs.

documents.title: Choose loading methods and table formats
documents.content: Loading design affects reliability and latency. Select batch or streaming processing and choose Delta, Parquet, CSV, JSON, or Iceberg based on transaction support, interoperability, schema, and performance requirements.

documents.title: Design data partitioning
documents.content: Partitioning can accelerate selective reads. Choose stable, appropriately sized partition columns based on common filters and data volume, while avoiding excessive cardinality and small files that increase metadata and processing overhead.

documents.title: Model changing and historical data
documents.content: Historical models preserve business change. Choose an appropriate slowly changing dimension type and use temporal tables, effective dates, current flags, or version records to answer point-in-time analytical questions.

documents.title: Choose granularity and table ownership
documents.content: Table design establishes meaning and ownership. Define a consistent row grain and column detail, then choose managed or unmanaged storage according to lifecycle control, interoperability, location, and governance requirements.

documents.title: Optimize table layout with clustering
documents.content: Physical layout influences query speed. Use liquid clustering or Z-ordering around common access patterns, and understand how deletion vectors improve row-level changes by delaying expensive file rewrites.

documents.title: Ingest with Lakeflow Connect and notebooks
documents.content: Databricks supports managed and custom ingestion. Lakeflow Connect simplifies supported batch and streaming sources, while Python, SQL, or Scala notebooks implement specialized extraction, parsing, transformation, and write logic.

documents.title: Ingest data with SQL
documents.content: SQL can load files and query results. Use CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, and COPY INTO for repeatable ingestion patterns with appropriate schemas, file options, and idempotency behavior.

documents.title: Process change data capture
documents.content: Change data capture processes source mutations efficiently. Consume inserts, updates, and deletes from a CDC feed, preserve ordering and keys, handle duplicates, and apply changes consistently to target Delta tables.

documents.title: Ingest streaming data
documents.content: Streaming ingestion processes continuous events. Spark Structured Streaming can read Azure Event Hubs and other sources using checkpoints, triggers, watermarks, and fault-tolerant sinks to provide scalable incremental processing.

documents.title: Use Auto Loader and declarative pipelines
documents.content: Auto Loader discovers arriving cloud files. Combine incremental file detection, schema inference and evolution, checkpoints, and Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines to create maintainable ingestion flows that scale with growing directories.

documents.title: Profile and clean source data
documents.content: Profiling reveals data problems early. Generate summary statistics and distributions, choose suitable column types, identify duplicate or missing records, and apply explicit rules to resolve null and invalid values.

documents.title: Filter, aggregate, and combine data
documents.content: Core transformations shape analytical datasets. Filter records, group and aggregate measures, join related tables, and use union, intersect, or except operations while preserving intended keys, cardinality, and semantics.

documents.title: Reshape and load transformed data
documents.content: Reshaping aligns data with consumption needs. Denormalize, pivot, or unpivot records, then load results through merge, insert, append, or overwrite operations selected for the required update and idempotency behavior.

documents.title: Implement data validation checks
documents.content: Validation prevents bad records from spreading. Check nullability, cardinality, numeric or date ranges, and expected data types, then reject, quarantine, repair, or report values that violate defined quality rules.

documents.title: Enforce schemas and pipeline expectations
documents.content: Schemas and expectations make quality explicit. Enforce compatible writes, manage intentional schema drift, and define Lakeflow pipeline expectations that warn, drop, or fail when records violate declared constraints.

category: Deploy and maintain pipelines and workloads

documents.title: Design pipeline operations
documents.content: Pipeline design defines reliable execution. Order extraction, validation, transformation, and publication steps according to dependencies, and choose notebooks or Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines based on complexity and operational needs.

documents.title: Design task logic and error handling
documents.content: Tasks need predictable failure behavior. Define inputs, outputs, dependencies, retries, timeouts, conditional paths, and recovery actions for notebooks, pipelines, and Lakeflow Jobs so errors remain observable and recoverable.

documents.title: Build notebook pipelines
documents.content: Notebook pipelines compose procedural tasks. Pass parameters and values between notebooks, configure precedence constraints and dependencies, isolate reusable logic, and make each step idempotent enough for safe retries or repair runs.

documents.title: Build lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines
documents.content: Declarative pipelines describe desired datasets. Define streaming tables, materialized views, transformations, dependencies, and quality expectations while Lakeflow manages orchestration, incremental processing, infrastructure, and operational state.

documents.title: Create and configure Lakeflow Jobs
documents.content: Lakeflow Jobs run production workflows. Create jobs with one or more dependent tasks, select compute, configure parameters and libraries, set permissions, and define execution settings appropriate to each workload.

documents.title: Configure job automation and recovery
documents.content: Automation keeps workloads timely and resilient. Configure event triggers or schedules, notify operators about failures or duration thresholds, and enable automatic restarts or retries that match the pipeline's recovery characteristics.

documents.title: Use Git development workflows
documents.content: Git supports collaborative Databricks development. Apply version-control practices, isolate changes in branches, review them through pull requests, and resolve merge conflicts before promoting notebooks and project files between environments.

documents.title: Test Databricks solutions
documents.content: Testing reduces deployment risk. Use unit tests for isolated logic, integration tests for connected components, end-to-end tests for complete workflows, and user acceptance testing to validate business requirements.

documents.title: Package and deploy Databricks bundles
documents.content: Bundles make deployment repeatable. Configure and package Databricks resources and source files as an Asset Bundle, define environment targets and variables, and deploy through the Databricks CLI or REST APIs.

documents.title: Monitor clusters and repair jobs
documents.content: Operational monitoring controls reliability and cost. Review cluster consumption and utilization, then diagnose Lakeflow Job runs and use repair, restart, stop, or rerun functions to recover failed workflows efficiently.

documents.title: Troubleshoot and optimize Spark workloads
documents.content: Spark diagnostics expose performance bottlenecks. Use execution DAGs, the Spark UI, and query profiles to investigate caching, skew, spilling, shuffles, resource pressure, slow stages, and failing jobs or notebooks.

documents.title: Optimize and maintain Delta tables
documents.content: Delta maintenance balances speed and storage cost. Use OPTIMIZE to compact small files and improve data layout, and apply VACUUM with a safe retention period to remove obsolete files.

documents.title: Stream logs and configure Azure Monitor alerts
documents.content: Centralized telemetry improves operations. Stream Azure Databricks logs to Log Analytics for querying and correlation, then configure Azure Monitor alert rules and action groups for important failures, thresholds, and service conditions.

documents.title: What is Azure Databricks?
documents.content: Azure Databricks is a unified analytics platform. It combines managed cloud infrastructure with tools for building, deploying, sharing, and maintaining enterprise data engineering, analytics, machine learning, and AI solutions at scale.

documents.title: The databricks runtime and Spark engine
documents.content: Apache Spark is a distributed processing engine on which Azure Databricks is built. It divides large data workloads across multiple compute nodes and provides APIs for SQL, Python, Scala, Java, machine learning, and real-time stream processing.

documents.title: What is a data lake?
documents.content: A data lake stores data at large scale. It keeps structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data in open file formats, often in inexpensive cloud object storage, for flexible downstream processing and analysis.

documents.title: What is a data warehouse?
documents.content: A data warehouse supports business analytics. It stores cleaned, structured, and integrated historical data in models optimized for SQL queries, reporting, dashboards, aggregation, and consistent decision-making across an organization.

documents.title: What is a data lakehouse?
documents.content: A data lakehouse combines lakes and warehouses. It provides low-cost, open storage for varied data together with reliable transactions, governance, performance, and structured analytics for BI, data science, and machine learning.

documents.title: What is Delta Lake?
documents.content: Delta Lake is an open storage layer. It adds a transaction log, ACID reliability, schema controls, scalable metadata, and unified batch and streaming support to Parquet data stored in a lakehouse.

documents.title: What is Unity Catalog?
documents.content: Unity Catalog is the Databricks governance layer. It centrally manages discovery, permissions, lineage, auditing, and secure access for data and AI assets across users, workspaces, and supported cloud storage locations.

documents.title: What is a Databricks workspace?
documents.content: A Databricks workspace is a collaborative environment. It provides the web interface and organizational boundary where teams create notebooks, queries, jobs, pipelines, dashboards, models, and other Databricks resources.

documents.title: What is a compute cluster?
documents.content: A compute cluster supplies processing resources. It groups a driver and worker nodes that run Spark commands, notebooks, and jobs, and can be configured or automatically scaled for workload requirements.

documents.title: What is a Databricks notebook?
documents.content: A Databricks notebook is an interactive document. It combines executable SQL, Python, Scala, or R cells with text, visualizations, parameters, and results for collaborative exploration, development, and scheduled processing.

documents.title: What is a SQL warehouse?
documents.content: A SQL warehouse is compute for SQL analytics. It runs queries, dashboards, and BI connections against lakehouse data, with sizing, scaling, and serverless options designed for concurrent analytical workloads.

documents.title: What is data engineering?
documents.content: Data engineering makes data usable. It involves ingesting, cleaning, transforming, modeling, securing, orchestrating, and monitoring data so reliable datasets are available for analytics, reporting, machine learning, and operational applications.

documents.title: What are ETL and ELT?
documents.content: ETL and ELT are data integration patterns. ETL transforms data before loading it into a destination, while ELT loads data first and uses the destination platform to perform transformations.

documents.title: Batch processing and stream processing
documents.content: Batch and streaming process data differently. Batch workloads handle bounded collections on a schedule, while streaming workloads continuously process arriving events to produce results with lower latency.

documents.title: What is medallion architecture?
documents.content: Medallion architecture refines data through layers. Bronze preserves raw ingested data, silver validates and cleans it, and gold presents enriched, aggregated, business-ready datasets for analytics and applications.

documents.title: What are ACID transactions?
documents.content: ACID properties make data operations reliable. Atomicity completes all changes or none, consistency preserves rules, isolation prevents concurrent interference, and durability ensures committed changes survive failures.
